description: We're Team Lumix — Matvey Meshkov and Ulyana Plukhina. We built Sol by Sol, a free 3D web app that opens Mars to everyone using real NASA data: HiRISE terrain, THEMIS thermal maps, and Perseverance's real path, samples and photos. We love space, maps and making science something you can explore with your own hands. Always happy to connect with people into planetary science, 3D graphics and design.
summary:
Sol by Sol is a free 3D web app that opens Mars to everyone. Built entirely from real NASA data, it turns Jezero Crater — where Perseverance is searching for signs of ancient life — into a place anyone can explore from a browser, no science background needed.

Visitors take a guided tour of ten real mission stops with the rover's own raw photos, replay Perseverance's real 45 km drive sol by sol, and switch between elevation, slope and THEMIS thermal layers. They can plan a safe route with an A* planner that estimates a crew Marswalk, then drive a concept crew rover across HiRISE terrain where slope, loose sand and energy all come from orbital data. At each site they read real measurements, identify the rock, and compare their answer with NASA's sample table.

The Martian Map challenge asks how to prepare the first crews. Our answer starts with everyone: by turning real mission data into exploration, Sol by Sol helps people understand Mars, the science behind it, and what it will take to walk there.
details:
We wanted anyone to be able to visit Mars — not an imagined one, but the real one. Sol by Sol is a free 3D web app that turns Jezero Crater into a world to explore. The terrain is built from the CTX digital elevation model at 20 m resolution and detailed HiRISE data down to 1 m. On top of it are the THEMIS thermal map, Perseverance's real 45 km path with 708 stops, 28 samples from NASA's sample table, and real images from the rover's cameras.

Users start with a tour of ten key mission moments, illustrated with the rover's own photos. Then they can replay Perseverance's drive sol by sol, switch between elevation, slope and thermal layers, or plan a safe route themselves. An A* algorithm avoids steep slopes and loose sand, and the app estimates a crew Marswalk: time, safety margin, turnaround point and radiation dose. Next, users take the wheel of a crew rover. Slope, loose ground and battery use all follow real data. At each station they read the measurements, identify the rock and check their answer against NASA, and at the end they compare their traverse with the algorithm and export a log of the drive.

The main benefit of the project is public outreach. Mars becomes open to everyone, with no science background, installation or registration needed. People don't just read about science — they do what scientists do: look at the data and make decisions. This brings real mission data to students and anyone curious about space, and helps them understand what the first humans will need to walk on Mars.

The app is written in JavaScript, with three.js for 3D; the data was processed with Node.js and geotiff.js. Data sources are USGS, NASA and JPL, the 3D models come from NASA 3D Resources, and the site is hosted on GitHub Pages and works on both desktop and mobile. We aimed to combine scientific accuracy with the feeling of being on Mars yourself. That's why everything we had to assume, such as the rover's parameters and walking pace, is clearly labeled in the app as an assumption.
